p:cNvPr.descr: Six diagrams that illustrate and describe the features of signal-transducing systems. Diagram A. In this diagram, a receptor is represented as a pink rectangle with a cutout on top. Small puzzle-like pieces labeled S1 and S2 that represent signal molecules are located above the rectangle with two way arrows between them and the rectangle. Underneath the rectangle, an arrow points down to Response. The text accompanying this diagram reads, "Specificity. Signal molecule fits binding site on its complementary receptor; other signals do not fit." Diagram B. In this diagram, an organizational chart-like diagram has three levels. Above each rectangle in the chart is a green triangle in a circle. Above the chart, the word Signal points with a down arrow to a single rectangle in the first row of the chart labeled Enzyme 1. This rectangle branches down to three rectangles in the second row, each labeled Enzyme 2. Each of these rectangle branches down to another three rectangles in the third row labeled Enzyme 3. The text accompanying the diagram reads, "Amplification. When enzymes activate enzymes, the number of affected molecules increase geometrically in an enzyme cascade." Diagram C. A vertical diagram begins with the word Signal on top with a down arrow pointing to three yellow circles connected by two lines arranged in the shape of the letter V. The vertex of the V is connected by a line down to a circle labeled P which sits inside a green oval with a cutout to hold the circle. The oval is connected by a line down to a circle labeled P, which sits inside of a pink rectangle with a cutout to hold the cirle. Below this rectangle is an arrow down to the word Response. The text accompanying the diagram reads, "Modularity. Proteins with multivarlent affinities form diverse signaling complexes from interchangable parts. Phosphorylation provides reversible points of interaction." Digram D. The word Signal is connected by a down arrow to a green triangle in a circle that sits atop a rectangle labeled Receptor. Under the rectangle, a downward arrow points to the word Response, while another arrow loops back up and left, and points to a red X in a circle that sits on the left side of the rectangle. The text accompanying the diagram reads, "Desensitization/Adaptation. Receptor activation triggers a feedback circuit that shuts off the receptor or removes it from the cell surface." Diagram E. This diagram has two side-by-side illustrations, one representing Signal 1, which has an arrow pointing down to a green triangle that sits atop a pink box representing Receptor 1, and the second representing Signal 2, which has an arrow pointing down to a green triangle ithat sits atop a pink oval representing Receptor 2. Under the illustration of Signal-Receptor 1 is the text, "[up arrow] [X] or [up-arrow] V-sub-m. Under the illustration of Signal-Receptor 2 is the text, "[down arrow] [X] or [down arrow] V-sub-m." A horizontal bracket points below to the text, "Net [delta]-[X] or [delta] V-sub-m," which is connected to a down arrow pointing to the text Response. The text accompanying the diagram reads, "Integration. When two signals have opposite effects on a metabolic characteristic such as the concentration of a second messenger X, or the membrane potential V-sub-m the regulatory outcome results from the integrated input from both receptors." Diagram F. A diagram representing a signal reaching a receptor is connected via a horizontal line from the Receptor. The signal points down to agreen rectangle in a circle which sits atop a pink rectangle representing the receptor. A line goes through the rectangle to a blue circle labeled Messenger Remover. An arrow below the Receptor points to the word message, and a curved arrow points from the word Message, tangents the Message remover, and points to word Message which has been crossed out with a red X. Underneath this arc is the text Response (local). The text accompanying the diagram reads, "Localized response. When the enzyme that destroys an intracellular message is clustered with the message producer, the message is degraded before it can diffuse to distant points, so the response is only local and brief."
